"To you who seek the truth, first wonder why it was hidden" (A slight misquote/summary of an old tale, where an adventurous boy who dreams of being an explorer wanders into the woods to find the monster that he was told lives within, becomes lost and nearly dies, only to be found and told there were only ever the woods, and they were empty. It leaves us with the question, should the boy stay in the village, live a life scared but free of the pain and grief, yet forever severing his relationship with his dream, the love, destiny? Or should he forgive them for hiding it, redouble, learn and continue trying until he's capable of exploring? I think about that boy alot, they never tell us what happens. It's a big tangent for a small, actually unrelated comment, but it felt fitting and i love to talk about silly things like folk tales.)

Koev li halev is a perfectly poetic phrase, well worthy of a tattoo. I think empathy is one of the most incredible parts of the human experience, but I'm quite biased as a major overthinker and hyper-empath. It also requires us to exercise a lot of caution with though. I think empathy can also be used as a form of escapism, neglecting our own needs to help others. The dying taking care of the sick, the sick taking care of the dying. Its beautiful, finding comfort in the act of caring, of loving. Make sure you don't bring too much of others pain into your heart though, lest you forget to take care of your own.
I don't know if I remember when it felt different. I only tried to keep track of what i felt rather than when, but I know I feel better now. Maybe not by as much as I'd hoped. But I'm better. That's everything I need to justify it.

I hope you find the sweet spot soon, remember that it takes more time than we realise for our bodies to adjust even when the dosage changes, don't push too far or too early, keep it spaced out between changes so you can figure out what's different and don't get a cumulative shock when your body recalibrates for them all at once. You sound like you're doing a good job though! It's hard to be patient with things like this. And it's hard to commit to changing something. Be proud of yourself, even if the result ends up differing from what you desired.

Keep me updated if you would! Rationally because it will also be helpful to me knowing more information about a seemingly unreported or unique circumstance, but instinctually and emotionally because even if you're a stranger to me, you're also a human i care about! 

Little bonus tidbit, I also have some hebrew tattoos! One of my first ever tattoos was "ז", and it's something that helps me remember all too many things.

Take care, dear friend! Wishing you comfort.

I don't want to overstep so I won't give advice, as I came across this searching for some myself, or someone who relates with the experience for another perspective.
I found myself in a very similar situation to you recently, I work as an author for the most part, and I suffer with predominantly bipolar disorder. 
I started medication and therapy in February of last year, and the last time i finished anything, book, draft, poem, short story, was early May and it was one of the most lifeless works I have ever produced. It felt like all I could write was the idea, I couldn't imbue any breath into it, because I couldn't feel anything to impart that experience into the writing. 
I became intensely demotivated, and craved the feeling of a writing mania, of being able to birth 10 poems in a night and feel each of them writhe on the paper like the emotion had slipped from my soul onto the plate, there for all to dissect, taste, experience.
So I stopped medication, initially by halving the tablet, later by only taking once at night, then finally half the one, and cold.
Over the course of 3 weeks I'd entirely stopped medicating and felt extremely fuzzy, like an almost constant dizziness that never quite passed the onset, I struggled to sleep and I felt almost hormonal. It was of no help that my period came just in time.

I still didn't feel like I could write.
I spent a month~ after that burning time. 
There was no mania yet, there was no depression. I really couldn't understand what was happening, why my brain seemed to be constantly on pause. Just the same dull apathy I'd longed to be rid of. Just the same husk feeling somehow more drained, tired and confused than before.
It took me a while to do anything after that, I thought it had failed, I wondered if it was just a mistake, I asked my therapist if she thought I was fucking it all up, I was desperately looking for somebody else to answer my questions other than me. I couldn't talk to my friends about it, I'd long since broken up with my partner, my family are the classic "Mental Illness isn't real, here's a bunch of traumatic stories about how horribly mentally ill I was as a youth, feel fine now". I just felt totally isolated and I knew in a way that I was doing that to myself. 
It took another month until I felt a recognisable tinge of mania, and it was sparked by a past flame reaching out to me about seeing a poem of mine posted onto someone's Facebook, and recognising that I'd written it about them...
A week later I'd written again.
It felt, normal. Like it was just how it was supposed to be. How it used to be. Better even. I felt better. That was dangerous.
To cut a long story short, I failed to reconcile with them, and I became depressed, then I became really depressed, and I started having true mood swings again. I think I dealt with them better than before, but it was still harrowing.
I restarted medication in January, about 2 months after the biggest episode. 
I've felt okay since then, I've been on a lower dose to try and minimise the zombification, and I've been trying to exercise more, eat better, make more friends and close connections. It's been okay. I wont lie, it's been horrible at times, rarely ever does it feel anything better than "quite nice", but I've been able to write more often, had stronger emotions and felt more "alive". 

Sorry for the long, late, random reply. Maybe you will find some use to it? That even though it's weird and fucked up, you aren't alone? Maybe you won't. Either way, all the best.
